## Tonight

By the time you leave this room you will have four programs installed, talking to each
other, and one file that proves it.

That is the whole goal. Everything else on these slides is me explaining why we bother.

## Let me be honest about tonight

- This is the least enjoyable evening of the semester. I am not going to pretend otherwise.
- Installing software is not research. It is the tedious part that makes research possible.
- **Something will break for somebody in this room.** It happens every section, every term.
- When it breaks it is not a verdict on you. It is one version number disagreeing with another.
- We fix it together, tonight, in the room. That is why we do it here and not at home.

## The reason, in one sentence

Six weeks from now you will look at a number in your own draft and not remember where it came from.

Everything tonight exists to make that impossible.

## What that looks like at scale

[Open Science Collaboration, 2015]{.eyebrow}

- 270 researchers set out to redo **100 published psychology studies**
- Same published methods, similar participants, same analyses
- Only **36 percent** replicated at conventional thresholds
- Among those that did, effect sizes averaged about **half** the original
- These were not careless people. Their work simply was not built to be retraced.

## What actually blocked them

- Not fraud. Ordinary friction.
- Methods sections did not say enough to re-run the analysis
- Researchers had to email the original authors to ask
- Some authors had moved. Some had lost the data.
- Some had used software whose menus had since changed

## Reproducibility, defined

**Reproducibility** means the analysis can be re-run, by you or by anyone else, and it
produces the same result.

It is not a virtue. It is a property of how you stored your work.

The test is small and personal: can you recover, six months from now, exactly what produced
a number?

## Why clicking loses

- SPSS, Excel, and JMP work through menus and dialog boxes
- You click Analyze, then Compare Means, then One-Way ANOVA. The result appears.
- **The click history vanishes.**
- Redoing it next month means remembering which menus, in what order, with which options
- Writing it down means describing every click in prose. Nobody does this well.

## Why code wins

A script is a description of every step, in a language a computer can re-run.

**The code is the methods section.** That is the entire argument for everything we install
tonight.

Reinhart and Rogoff, the spreadsheet error from last week, was caught only because the file
was eventually shared. Written as code, it would have been visible from the first day.

## Tool 1 of 4: VS Code

**What it is:** a text editor. Free, from Microsoft.

**What it does for you:** it is the one window where everything lives. Your writing, your
code, your files, your output. You stop alt-tabbing between five programs.

You will spend more time in this than in anything else this term. It is the desk, not the work.

## Tool 2 of 4: R

**What it is:** a programming language built for data and statistics.

**What it does for you:** it counts things, tests things, and draws charts, and it leaves a
written record of having done so.

You are not becoming a programmer. You are learning to drive one tool for one job, the way
you learned to drive a citation manager.

## Tool 3 of 4: Quarto

**What it is:** a publishing system.

**What it does for you:** you write one file holding both your prose and your code, press
render, and it produces a finished document with the charts already in place.

No more pasting a chart into Word, finding an error, redoing the chart, and pasting it again.

## Tool 4 of 4: Git and GitHub

**What it is:** Git records every change you make. GitHub keeps that record online.

**What it does for you:** an undo button that reaches back months, and proof of when you did what.

It is also the closest thing our field has to a portfolio. Employers look. Use a professional
username.

## Install in this order

1. **R**, from cran.r-project.org
2. **VS Code**, from code.visualstudio.com
3. **The R extension** inside VS Code, by REditorSupport
4. **Quarto**, from quarto.org
5. **The Quarto extension** inside VS Code
6. **Git**, from git-scm.com

The order is not decorative. Each one looks for the one before it and gets confused when it
is missing.

## Now open the file I sent you

`00-check-your-setup.qmd` is on the Hub and in your email.

Open it in VS Code. It walks you through the rest, one grey box at a time, and it tells you
what each box should print.

Work through it. I am coming round the room. Raise a hand the moment something looks wrong,
not at the end.

## What "working" looks like

The file finishes by running a checker we wrote for this course:

```r
library(v2v)
setup()
```

You want a list of green check marks under **Required R packages**.

Red marks next to Quarto or Git are expected tonight if you have not finished those steps.
Red under Required is the one that needs me.

## When it breaks

- **Red text in R is not automatically an error.** R prints ordinary progress in red. Read
  the last line, not the colour.
- Close VS Code completely and reopen it. This genuinely fixes a lot.
- If R asks "which would you like to update", type 1 and press Enter.
- Send me the exact wording of the error, not a paraphrase. The wording is the diagnosis.
- Fifteen minutes stuck, then ask. Not two hours.

## Discussion {.discuss}

On Wilson et al. (2017), "Good enough practices in scientific computing":

- The title concedes something. What work is "good enough" doing, and who is it for?
- Which of their practices would survive contact with your actual working habits, and which
  would you quietly abandon by October?
- They write for the researcher with no formal computing training. Does that framing make the
  advice more usable, or does it lower the ceiling?
- Bring one practice you think is oversold.

*Two minutes with a neighbor, then we compare.*

## First contact with the data

[stream_log, November 2018]{.eyebrow}

| channel | game | viewers | date |
|---|---|--:|--:|
| sodapoppin | Marble It Up! | 27,934 | 1542578200214 |
| xqcow | Just Chatting | 19,381 | 1542578200240 |
| forsen | Artifact | 15,300 | 1542578200273 |
| giantwaffle | Rocket League | 4,697 | 1542578200423 |
| sodapoppin | Marble It Up! | 28,076 | 1542578261145 |
| xqcow | Just Chatting | 19,231 | 1542578261186 |

Look before you read on. Resist doing anything with it.

## The data moves

- This is a **time series**, not a snapshot. Four channels recur across these rows.
- Sodapoppin climbs 27,934, then 28,076, then 28,203
- That is **269 viewers in 122 seconds**, an audience growing close to real time
- xQc lost 150 between the first two snapshots, then held. Forsen lost 120.
- Each number is a real moment: a clip went viral, a raid arrived, bandwidth dropped

## The timestamps are not dates

- That date column is a thirteen-digit integer: 1542578200214
- The next row, 26 milliseconds later, reads 1542578200240
- **Unix epoch time**: milliseconds since midnight, January 1, 1970
- The gap between sodapoppin's first two rows is 60,931, about a minute
- Converting it is a wrangling step, not a research question. Chapter 11 handles it.

## Titles are themselves data

- xQc: "RANK 1 GAMER ~ NO PLAN (help me)", which is a joke
- Forsen is giving away keys for a card game called Artifact
- Giantwaffle performs etiquette: "No Smoking in Chat"
- One title even carries a literal line break, because the streamer's software let it through
- These are content analysis opportunities sitting in a column you might dismiss as metadata

## What the package gives you

- `twitch_chat_sample`: roughly **35,000** chat messages from a 50-channel corpus
- `twitch_streams_sample`: the stream snapshots for those channels, about **32,000** rows
- Helpers that wrap loading, codebook skeletons, reliability metrics, and diagnostics
- The helpers are not magic. They keep the concept from being buried under setup code.
- `setup()` re-runs any time you suspect an installation problem

## Lock the versions

`renv.lock` is a file recording the exact version of every package your analysis used.

Without it, someone re-running your work next year may get different numbers, because a
package changed underneath them and nobody noticed.

```r
renv::init()
```

Run it before your first line of analysis code. Commit it before you collect your first data point.

> "Back up (almost) everything created by a human being as soon as it is created. This includes scripts and programs of all kinds, software packages that your project depends on, and documentation."
>
> Wilson et al. (2017, p. 12)
